Kratom (Mitragynia speciosa Korth) is a tree-like plant native to Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, and other parts of southeast Asia. Indigenous users create a “juice” by boiling fresh kratom leaves for several hours that is then diluted with hot water to make kratom tea. Kratom is used in traditional environments to treat diarrhea, hypertension, cough, fever, impotence, and other ailments. Kratom is used by manual laborers for its mild stimulant effects, a replacement remedy for individuals with problematic opioid use, and as a mild analgesic agent. In the west, many different kratom formulations are available, including tinctures, extracts, capsules, softgels, concentrated products, as well as dried leaf powders and cut leaf material. 5

December 18, 2025 Page 6 Kratom in western countries is most commonly used as a remedy for opioid addiction, chronic pain, depression, and anxiety. 19. The neurobehavioral effects of kratom are more subtle than the commonly described stimulant effects at low doses and opioid effects at higher doses. Low doses of kratom increase alertness, energy, and talkativeness. At doses greater than 5 grams, however, kratom users describe the persistence of heightened alertness coupled with analgesia. These effects account for the use of kratom as a mild stimulant for manual laborers, a replacement remedy for individuals with problematic opioid use, and as a mild analgesic agent. 20. Some of the biological effects of kratom arise from binding of alkaloidal components to a number of neurotransmitter receptors in the central nervous system, including the µ-opioid (MOR), κ-opioid, serotonergic (5-HT), and alpha (α1) receptors, among others. MOR activity is particularly important. MOR activation mediates pain, respiratory rate, gastrointestinal transit time, nausea, and pruritis, among other effects. Each of these effects is mediated via distinct signaling pathways following binding of an agonist to the MOR receptor. 21. Classical opioid agonists (e.g., morphine and fentanyl) are “unbiased” agonists in that they indiscriminately activate all biological effects mediated by MOR. Kratom is different. The most prevalent—and best studied—alkaloid in kratom is mitragynine. In contrast to classical unbiased MOR agonists, mitragynine is a “biased” agonist in that it produces some, but not all, effects that arise from receptor binding of a classical MOR agonist such as morphine or fentanyl. 22. For example, while mitragynine produces analgesia, it does not produce the stupor characteristic of classic, unbiased MOR agonists. Instead, kratom produces increased alertness. Furthermore, mitragynine does not produce the respiratory depression that is a leading cause of mortality from classical unbiased MOR agonist overdose (Macko 1972; Varadi 2016; Kruegel 2019; Boyer 2012). 23. In fact, the clinical features as well as the time course of the toxidrome from kratom has never been described. Testing for mitragynine is generally limited to commercial forensic companies and medical examiner offices. Mitragynine itself undergoes postmortem redistribution; the postmortem concentration of mitragynine measured by forensic laboratories is over three times higher than premortem blood. 24. In general, adverse events attributed to kratom have been derived from database studies, poorly controlled case reports, or small case series, each of which has serious deficiencies in patient background information, including medical, social, or family history; clinical evaluation; scene findings; or analytical technique. These poorly controlled studies at times associate kratom with agitation, seizures, liver injury, renal injury, ventricular dysrhythmia, and respiratory depression. Individually and collectively, these studies lack the scientific heft to establish causation between kratom use and any adverse event. 25. No evidence supports the contention that Harmony Moller’s use of kratom contributed to her death. The postmortem concentration of mitragynine identified in Ms. Moller’s blood was 158 ng/mL as measured by the Gerona lab (St. Tammany Parish Coroner records); commercial clinical laboratories measured the mitragynine concentration as 150 ng/mL (St. Tammany Parish Coroner records). Mitragynine undergoes postmortem redistribution, a process where the concentration of a substance changes following death. The available scientific literature demonstrates that the postmortem concentration of mitragynine is approximately triple that of pre- mortem measurements (Osawa 2025). To a reasonable degree of medical certainty, therefore, Ms. Moller’s premortem concentration of mitragynine was approximately 50 ng/mL, a value that occurred in human clinical trials involving kratom. Notably, none of the participants in these studies developed cardiac toxicity, much less a life-threatening event. Ms. Moller did not die from her kratom use. 76. In fact, medical examiners initially noted that the cause of death was “chronic liver congestion.” Chronic liver congestion is a medical condition often associated with right heart failure; backup of blood (i.e., “congestion”) into the liver produces fibrotic changes that become apparent even on visual inspection of the liver. Notably, kratom has not been associated with chronic liver congestion, even among patients where right heart failure was putatively associated with distant and undefined kratom ingestion (Alameh 2025). 77. Although I agree with the medical examiner’s finding that Ms. Moller died from complications of her unrecognized congenital heart disease—that has a recognized association with sudden cardiac death—I find that the medical examiner errs in failing to consider adequately the pharmacophysiology of the full range of substances identified on postmortem testing. 78. I find that the medical examiner errs in determining that Harmony Moller’s kratom use contributed to her death. In fact, the pharmacophysiology of kratom is more likely to be protective against cardiac sudden death in a patient such as Ms. Moller who had a high takeoff of the coronary artery with an acute angle of origin complicated by an inferior aortic flap. Following ingestion, mitragynine exerts parasympathetic effects on the cardiovascular system (Saengmolee 2022; Prevete 2024). These effects, measured generally as a slight decrease in systolic and diastolic blood pressure even in the setting of greater alertness, are insufficient to contribute to morbidity and mortality of an individual with high takeoff of the coronary artery with an acute angle of origin of the coronary artery complicated by an inferior aortic flap (Saengmolee 2022; Prevete 2024).1 79. I also find that the medical examiner errs in ignoring other substances more likely than mitragynine to worsen the congenital heart disease described in the medical record. Normally, the aorta has “elasticity,” meaning it can dilate slightly during a pulse of blood from the heart. Harmony Moller ingested caffeine. Caffeine is an over-the-counter stimulant that increases pulse rate and intra-aortic blood pressure, but caffeine also limits the elasticity (i.e., how much the blood vessel can expand in response to increased blood pressure) of the aorta. Caffeine’s pharmacologic actions make it dangerous in a person with high takeoff of the left coronary artery with an acute angle of origin. Caffeine increases aortic blood pressure and decreases aortic elasticity. These direct pharmacologic effects of caffeine compress the opening of the coronary artery precisely because the coronary artery has an acute angle of origin that narrows as the aorta expands (Virmani 1984). Moreover, the inferior aortic flap is an additional obstruction to blood flow into the coronary artery as the increased aortic blood pressure caused by caffeine presses it against the wall of the aorta. Ms. Moller’s caffeine use occluded the coronary artery and hindered blood flow into heart muscle. This decrease in cardiac perfusion caused a malignant arrhythmia culminating in sudden cardiac death. Caffeine, not mitragynine, exacerbated Ms. Moller’s congenital heart disease and contributed to her death. 80. Even if Ms. Moller was not taking her caffeine supplements, she also had “Mini Thins,” a weight-loss remedy. This product contains caffeine and yohimbine, among other plant products. Yohimbine is a presynaptic alpha-2 antagonist. The pharmacologic effects of yohimbine are to increase pulse rate and blood pressure. These direct pharmacologic effects of yohimbine, either with or without caffeine, compress the opening of the coronary artery precisely because the coronary artery has an acute angle of origin that narrows as the aorta expands (Virmani 1984). 81. Even if Harmony Moller did not die of her congenital heart disease complicated by her caffeine use, she had other, more plausible causes of death than mitragynine toxicity. For example, Ms. Moller’s vomiting was so severe that Kathleen Moller administered multiple antiemetics without improvement. Harmony Moller was taking two different caffeine-containing supplements. Caffeine is a methylxanthine. The methylxanthine toxidrome involves vomiting, seizure, and ventricular dysrthythmias (Shimane 2017). Death in methylxanthine-poisoned individuals arises from seizures or from malignant ventricular dysrhythmias (Shimane 2017; Poussel 2013). The medical examiner failed to quantify the postmortem concentration of caffeine even though Harmony Moller’s clinical presentation (i.e., severe vomiting despite multiple antiemetics before being found down with no anatomic cause of death other than her congenital heart disease) was consistent with lethal methylxanthine poisoning. This clinical presentation is also inconsistent with mitragynine toxicity. 82. Harmony Moller did not die from any contribution of mitragynine to her congenital heart disease. 83. Harmony Moller did not die from mitragynine toxicity 84. Harmony Moller did not die from her kratom use. 85. My clinical contributions, the most important of which have been published in high-impact general medical journals, have been adopted internationally by clinicians working in emergency medicine, medical toxicology, pediatrics, infectious diseases, psychiatry, addiction medicine, and behavioral science. My research career, supported continuously by NIH since 2001 and informed by observations I make as a bedside clinician, has emphasized two main areas of investigation. In a series of studies from 2007, I have pioneered the use of signal processing and machine learning to identify, in real time and in natural environments, relapse to cocaine use, behavioral transitions to increased health risk, emerging population-wide drug use behaviors, and the opioid sparing effect of machine learning-tagged music. My second field of study involves advanced technologies in health. My studies related to mobile biosensors have provided vivid, indisputable evidence of medication ingestion, detected opioid use as well as the development of opioid tolerance, and apps that modulate pain and anxiety. Recognizing the innovativeness of my science and its impact on multiple scientific disciplines, NIH awarded me a K24 mid-career award—the first emergency physician to be so funded—so that I could mentor junior faculty into skilled clinician-scientists. This funding led to a flowering of my academic career as the scope of my research expanded even further. My research grown to include web semantic learning to identify new patterns of psychoactive substance use, Bluetooth- labeled naloxone syringes to determine the fate of opioid antidote distributed into the community, and ingestible biosensors that measure, rather than infer, the actual time at which patients take their medications, and the study of machine learning-tagged music as an intervention for pain and anxiety. One outgrowth of my mentoring efforts has been improvements in academic practice and the study of methods to accelerate academic productivity. My initial effort in this area emphasized writing retreats that focused on providing a linkage of junior authors to senior faculty; follow up work focused on establishing iterative writing periods where participating junior faculty provided critiques and writing suggestions for others’ work. By replacing a didactic approach to authorship with faster support and editorial review, this fundamental advance accelerated the academic careers of junior faculty, particularly those of female faculty. I have also extended my mentoring work to the study of resident wellness where I led a study evaluating commercial sound-cancelling sleepbuds to help clinicians transition to and recover from overnight shifts. The innovation of my work has been recognized by four different academic disciplines. First, I was named the 2008 NIH Distinguished Lecturer in Natural Products Neurosciences, an award from the medicinal chemistry community for my studies related to adverse effects of kratom. Then, in 2011, I received the American College of Medical Toxicology’s annual Research Award for career accomplishments in research investigations. My studies to extend the capacity of wearable biosensors into drug abuse treatment was applauded by the Society of Behavioral Medicine with the 2015 Citation Award. In 2016, I was the overall winner of the Medstro Innovations in Healthcare Challenge for my work related to digital pills for medication ingestion monitoring. Finally, in 2018 I was named a Fulbright Scholar to Malaysia to study the pharmacophysiology of kratom in Malaysian heroin injectors.
